blocks.t: A script is a sentence you carry about yourself that you treat as true without examining.
blocks.h: A script is a sentence you carry about yourself that you treat as true without examining.

blocks.t: You have several. Everyone does. Some of them are useful and accurate. I am a person who likes the color blue. I am a person who is funny with my close friends. I am a person who is good at remembering song lyrics. Those scripts are fine. Those scripts are descriptive. Those scripts can keep doing their job.

blocks.t: The scripts we are concerned with in this chapter are the ones that are not descriptive — the ones that are judgmental, and global, and delivered to you in a voice that was not yours to begin with.

blocks.t: Read those slowly. If your eyes caught on one of them — if your body did something at one of them, a small constricting feeling, a yes — that is information. That sentence is in your file. You did not put it there. But it is there now, and it is running quietly underneath everything you do, and it is shaping the way you experience your own life.

blocks.t: Here is the painful thing about scripts.
blocks.h: Here is the painful thing about scripts.

blocks.t: Most of them were not written by you.
blocks.h: Most of them were not written by you.

blocks.t: Most of them were written by somebody in your life, at some point, often before you were old enough to know what was being written. A parent who, in a stressed moment, said the wrong thing — and it was an aberration, and they did not mean it, but it landed, and the seven-year-old version of you wrote it down. A teacher who singled you out, on a bad day, in front of a class — and you wrote down what their face said about you. A grandparent, an aunt, a coach, an older sibling, a kid in second grade who teased you for one specific thing — anyone, at any moment, who delivered a sentence about you that you absorbed and have been quietly carrying ever since.

blocks.t: Sometimes the scripts were not delivered by a single person, but by a system. The way your school treated kids who looked like you. The way the media depicted people from your community. The way the adults around you talked about the kind of family you came from, or the kind of body you had, or the way you learned, or did not learn. Systemic scripts are harder to identify because they do not have a single author — they come from the air — but they are no less real, and they are often the heaviest ones in the file.

blocks.t: Theo wrote, in pencil, in his notebook:
blocks.h: Theo wrote, in pencil, in his notebook:

blocks.t: Section 1. The script: I am the one who watches. I am not the one who is watched.
blocks.h: Section 1. The script: I am the one who watches. I am not the one who is watched.

blocks.t: Section 2. Where it came from: I do not know exactly. I think it started somewhere around second grade. I was small for my grade. I was quiet. The teachers, when they were dividing the class for things, would always put me with kids who needed somebody to watch them. I think I was being trained, in some way, to be a watcher. It also might have been the family. My parents have always asked me to look out for my sister Lena, who is older than I am but who has been — I do not have the word for this — Lena is the kind of older sister who needs looking out for, not the kind who looks out. So I have, since I was small, been the noticing one. I think the script is that I am not the protagonist of any room. I am the kid in the background watching the room. The protagonist is somebody else.

blocks.t: Section 4. What it costs me to keep it: I am tired. The watching is tiring. I do it whether or not I am being paid attention to. I am, in some real way, watching the room even at the cohort lunch table. The cost is that I do not get to ever fully relax. The watcher is always on duty.

To make jokes you did not know in advance would land. To, occasionally, be the kid in the cohort who is carried rather than the kid who carries.

blocks.t: The script does not vanish in one afternoon. The script is twelve years old. The script is going to keep showing up, in small ways, for years. But Theo has, today, put it on a piece of paper, and named it, and told another person about it. Those three steps are, in some real way, the beginning of every script-rewriting that has ever happened.
